title: Patch Clamp and the Rise of Optogenetics: Over Two Decades of Research on HEKA Amplifiers
body_markdown:
Neuroscientists have long faced a basic limitation: electrical stimulation can activate brain tissue, and drugs can modulate it, but neither can target a single genetically defined cell type with millisecond precision. Optogenetics, which uses light-gated ion channels to switch specific neurons on or off, was developed to close that gap. This year, Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for that work.


### From Algal Photoreceptors to Neural Control


Nagel and Hegemann showed that channelrhodopsins, light receptors from the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, are ion channels opened directly by light (1, 2). Deisseroth's group then expressed channelrhodopsin-2 in mammalian neurons and showed that brief light pulses could drive reliable, millisecond-timed action potentials (3). Within a few years, opsins had become standard tools for linking defined neurons to circuits and behavior.


### Why Patch Clamp Matters for Optogenetics


Every new opsin has to be characterized electrically before it can be trusted as a tool. Whole-cell patch clamp remains the standard method for measuring:


- Photocurrent amplitude and kinetics
- Ion selectivity and reversal potential
- Wavelength sensitivity of color-tuned variants
- Fidelity of light-evoked action potentials
- Synaptic responses in optogenetically defined circuits


In circuit studies, patch clamp also confirms that light activates the intended neurons and that downstream effects are synaptic rather than artefacts of illumination.


### HEKA Amplifiers in the Laureates' Research


A literature review by HEKA's applications team identified 18 peer-reviewed papers from the laureates' groups that name HEKA patch clamp amplifiers in their methods. They span from 2005 to 2026 and include work published in Nature, Cell, Neuron and PNAS. The studies cover:


- Channelrhodopsin structure and ion selectivity
- Red-shifted and color-tuned opsins
- Calcium indicators combined with optogenetics
- Nanoscale optogenetics
- Hypothalamic circuits for thirst and wakefulness
- Circuits for fear extinction and aversion
- All-optical voltage clamp of muscles and neurons in live C. elegans


The full list appears under Featured Research below.


### From EPC 7 to EPC 10 USB


The earlier studies used EPC 7 and EPC 9 amplifiers with Pulse software. More recent work used the EPC 10 USB (the latest iteration of which is the[EPC 10 USB 3.0](https://heka.com/products/products_main.html#physiol_comp) ) with[PATCHMASTER NEXT software](https://heka.com/products/products_main.html#soft_pm_next) . The EPC 10 USB 3.0 amplifiers provide multiple digital lines and 3 analogue output channels for controlling light sources in optogenetic experiments. The software PATCHMASTER NEXT with its optional extensions[SmartLUX](https://www.heka.com/products/products_main.html#control_imaging_soft) or[DocuLUX](https://www.heka.com/products/products_main.html#control_docu) integrates electrophysiological data recording with synchronized light-excitation and image acquisition. Complex experimental patterns can be designed and repetitively executed using the protocol editor.


### Conclusion


Optogenetics changed how neuroscientists study circuits and behaviour, and electrophysiology has been part of that work since the first experiments. HEKA congratulates Professors Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, and thanks the many researchers who report their instrumentation in their methods so others can reproduce their work.
